axolotl.anatomy: An axolotl's most striking features are the three pairs of feathery gills that sweep back from its head. Each stalk is fringed with fine filaments that are packed with blood vessels, which is why they often look pink or red; the more filaments, the more oxygen it can pull from the water. Its eyes are small and lidless, and its eyesight is poor, so it relies heavily on smell and on a lateral line, a row of pressure-sensitive cells along each side that feels the faint ripples made by moving prey. Wild axolotls are dark, mottled olive and brown with gold flecks, ideal for hiding on a muddy bed. The pale pink, golden and white axolotls in pet shops come from captive lines. Its teeth are tiny cones used to grip rather than chew, so prey is swallowed whole. Unusually, it carries a huge genome: about ten times more DNA than a human.
axolotl.family: Axolotls breed in the cool months, from roughly December to June. A courting male nudges the female and performs a sort of slow waggling dance, then deposits small packets of sperm on the lake bed. The female picks one up with her cloaca and later lays between a few hundred and around a thousand eggs, sticking them one by one to water plants and stones. The eggs hatch after about two weeks into tiny larvae that must start hunting almost immediately, first on microscopic animals, then on larger prey as they grow. Neither parent looks after the young, and adults will eat eggs and larvae, including their own. Axolotls can breed when they are about a year old. In captivity, a single female may spawn several times a year, which is one reason the species is so common in laboratories even while it vanishes in the wild.
axolotl.people: The Aztecs ate axolotls and featured them in their stories, and for centuries they were sold in Mexico City markets as food and medicine. European scientists first saw living axolotls in 1864, when a batch was sent to Paris. To everyone's astonishment, a few of them later transformed into land-dwelling salamanders, revealing that the axolotl could change but normally doesn't. Since then it has become one of the most studied amphibians in the world, used in research on regeneration, embryos and cancer. In modern Mexico it is a cultural icon: it appears on the 50-peso banknote, in murals, festivals and toys, and has a museum devoted to it in Chapultepec Park. Scientists from the National Autonomous University of Mexico work with local farmers in Xochimilco to keep canals clean and create refuges, and visitors can 'adopt' an axolotl to fund the work.

monarch-butterfly.anatomy: Like all butterflies, a monarch has four wings covered in thousands of tiny overlapping scales, which create its orange and black pattern. You can tell males from females by looking at the hind wings: males have a small black spot on a vein of each hind wing, made of special scent scales, and slightly thinner black veins. Monarchs taste with their feet, which helps a female check that a leaf is milkweed before laying an egg on it. Adults feed through a long, coiled tube called a proboscis that unrolls to sip nectar. Their compound eyes can see ultraviolet light, and the clock genes in their antennae are essential to navigation: in experiments, monarchs with painted-over antennae lose their sense of direction. The striped caterpillar has two pairs of black tentacles, one at each end, which it uses to feel its way and may help confuse predators.
monarch-butterfly.family: A female monarch lays each egg singly, usually on the underside of a young milkweed leaf, and may lay several hundred over her short life. The egg hatches in three to five days. The caterpillar's first meal is its own eggshell, then it starts on the milkweed, carefully chewing a circle to drain the leaf's sticky latex before eating. It sheds its skin four times as it grows. After about two weeks, it hangs head-down in a J shape and forms its chrysalis, which turns from jade green to see-through just before the adult emerges, roughly ten to fourteen days later. Summer butterflies mate and lay eggs within days. The autumn generation is different: shorter days and cooler temperatures switch off breeding, so these butterflies put all their energy into migrating and surviving the winter, mating only when spring arrives.
monarch-butterfly.people: For centuries, people in central Mexico knew that millions of butterflies appeared each November, around the Day of the Dead, and many saw them as the returning souls of ancestors. Scientists didn't know where North America's monarchs went until 1975, when a team following decades of tagging work by Canadian zoologist Fred Urquhart found the overwintering forests in the mountains west of Mexico City. Today part of that area is protected as the Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and tourism provides local communities with income. Citizen scientists across Canada and the United States tag monarchs with tiny stickers, count them at milkweed patches, and plant 'waystations' of milkweed and nectar flowers in gardens and schoolyards. The monarch is also the official insect or butterfly of several US states, and a symbol of the three countries working together to protect it.

rusty-patched-bumble-bee.anatomy: Rusty patched bumble bees are round, fuzzy bees with mostly yellow and black bands. Queens are larger than workers and lack the rusty patch, which is why identification needs a close look. Their dense hair keeps them warm and collects pollen, which they comb into pollen baskets on their hind legs, flat shiny areas fringed with stiff hairs. Like other bumble bees, they have a fairly long tongue for reaching nectar deep inside flowers. Females have a smooth stinger they can use more than once, but bumble bees are gentle and sting only when handled or when their nest is threatened. They see ultraviolet light and patterns on petals that are invisible to us, and they can even sense the weak electric charge of a flower, which changes briefly after another bee has visited, helping them skip flowers that have just been emptied.
rusty-patched-bumble-bee.family: Each spring, a mated queen emerges from her winter hideaway in loose soil and searches for a nest site, often an abandoned rodent burrow. She builds a wax pot of nectar and a small mound of pollen, lays her first eggs on it, and keeps them warm by shivering her flight muscles and pressing her body against the brood, much like a bird on its nest. These first daughters become workers, taking over foraging while the queen stays home to lay eggs. Rusty patched colonies grow large for bumble bees and remain active into autumn. Late in the season, the colony switches to raising males and new queens. They leave to mate, the old queen and her workers die as the weather cools, and only the young queens dig in for the winter, carrying the next year's colonies inside them.
rusty-patched-bumble-bee.people: The rusty patched bumble bee was once so common that few people noticed it. Its collapse was spotted in the late 1990s by researchers studying bumble bees in the US Midwest, and in 2017 it became the first bumble bee, and the first bee in the continental United States, to be listed as endangered. In Canada it is listed as Endangered under the Species at Risk Act, and surveys continue in southern Ontario in the hope that it still survives there. Much of what we know about its current range comes from volunteers: projects such as Bumble Bee Watch ask people to photograph bumble bees and upload them so experts can identify them. Gardeners can help by planting native flowers like wild bergamot, goldenrod and asters, leaving some leaf litter and bare ground, and avoiding pesticides.

luna-moth.anatomy: Luna moths belong to the giant silk moths, a family of big, heavy-bodied moths. Their wings are a soft lime green, edged with a band of purple or brown in the north and yellow in the south, and each wing carries a transparent eyespot that may startle predators. The long hind-wing tails twist as the moth flies. Males have very broad, feathery antennae covered in sensors that can detect a few molecules of a female's scent; females have narrower antennae. Adults have no working mouth and a reduced digestive system, since they never feed. The caterpillar is bright green with small red or yellow bumps, and grows to about 7 centimetres. When threatened it rears up, clicks its jaws and may regurgitate a bitter fluid. Its colour matches the leaves it eats so well that most people never notice one.
luna-moth.family: Female luna moths release their scent, called a pheromone, after dark, usually around midnight, and males fly in from far away. They mate through the early morning. The next evening the female begins laying around 200 to 300 eggs, in small groups on the leaves of the trees her caterpillars will eat. The eggs hatch after about a week. The caterpillars molt five times over several weeks, eating heavily. When fully grown, a caterpillar spins a thin silk cocoon wrapped in leaves, which usually falls to the forest floor. In Canada, the luna moth spends the winter as a pupa inside this cocoon, hidden in the leaf litter, and the adult emerges in late spring or early summer. Further south, summer generations follow one another quickly, and the last of the year overwinters the same way.
luna-moth.people: The luna moth was named in the 1700s after the Roman moon goddess Luna, for its pale colour and night flights. It has become one of the most recognisable moths in North America and a favourite of photographers and nature lovers, appearing on a 1987 US postage stamp. Because the adults are so short-lived and only active at night, seeing one is often a memorable event. Like many night-flying insects, luna moths are drawn to artificial light, where they waste precious time and energy and are easier for birds and bats to catch. Many conservation groups now recommend turning off unnecessary outdoor lights or using warm, shielded bulbs. Keeping native trees such as birch, walnut and hickory, and leaving fallen leaves under them over the winter, protects the cocoons that are resting there until spring.

common-loon.anatomy: The common loon has a long, dagger-shaped bill, a black head with a glossy green sheen in summer, a striped white necklace, and a black-and-white checkerboard back. Its eyes are a deep red, which may help it see underwater, where red light fades quickly. Loons have special muscles that change the shape of their lenses, so they can focus both in air and underwater. Their bones are solid rather than hollow, and they can squeeze air out of their feathers and lungs to sink quietly. Their legs sit so far back that they cannot easily walk, but they make loons powerful underwater swimmers that chase fish with their feet. Their wings are small for their weight, which is why they need a long run across the water to take off. In the air, though, loons are fast fliers, reaching speeds of over 100 km/h.
common-loon.family: Loons usually pair up with the same partner for several years and return to the same lake. They build a simple nest of plants right at the water's edge, because they can barely walk, and lay one or two olive-brown eggs. Both parents take turns incubating for about four weeks. Chicks can swim almost immediately but ride on their parents' backs for the first couple of weeks to rest and stay warm. Both parents feed them small fish and insects, and the chicks learn to dive and catch their own food over the summer. By around 11 or 12 weeks, the young can fly. In autumn the adults leave first, and the young follow later on their own. Young loons stay on the ocean for two or three years before returning north to breed.
common-loon.people: Loons have long been important in Indigenous stories across North America. In some Anishinaabe traditions the loon is a clan animal, and its calls appear in many legends. To settlers and cottagers, the loon's wail came to symbolise the northern wilderness, and it appears on the Canadian one-dollar coin, introduced in 1987, which gave the coin its nickname 'loonie'. It is Ontario's provincial bird and Minnesota's state bird. Loons are sensitive indicators of lake health. Many are poisoned after swallowing lead sinkers or jigs, which they mistake for the pebbles they swallow to help digestion, so several provinces and states encourage or require lead-free tackle. Volunteers across Canada take part in loon surveys each summer, counting pairs and chicks to track how lakes are doing.

atlantic-puffin.anatomy: An Atlantic puffin is a small, chunky seabird with a black back, white belly and white face. In summer its large, triangular bill is striped with blue, yellow and bright orange, with a fleshy yellow rosette at the corners of the mouth. Small dark horn-like plates above and below its eyes give it a sad expression. Puffins' bills even glow under ultraviolet light, which other puffins may be able to see. Their wings are short and strong, built more for 'flying' underwater than in the air, so they must flap very fast to stay aloft. Underwater they use their wings to pursue fish and their orange feet to steer, and they can dive down to around 60 metres, although most dives are much shallower. Spines on the roof of the mouth and a rough tongue hold caught fish in place while the puffin keeps hunting.
atlantic-puffin.family: Puffins usually return to the same mate and the same burrow every year, greeting each other by tapping and rubbing their bills together, a display called billing. They dig their burrows up to about a metre long using their bills and feet, or take over rabbit holes, and line the nest chamber with grass and feathers. The female lays a single white egg, and both parents take turns incubating it for about six weeks. The chick, called a puffling, is fed small fish several times a day. After about six weeks in the dark burrow, the puffling leaves at night, flying or tumbling down to the sea, and swims away from land. It spends its first few years entirely at sea and returns to the colony when it is around three to five years old, first breeding at about five.
atlantic-puffin.people: People in Iceland, the Faroe Islands and Norway have hunted puffins for food for centuries, using long-handled nets to catch birds in flight, and in some places limited hunting continues today. In the 1800s and early 1900s, hunting wiped out puffin colonies on many islands in the Gulf of Maine. In 1973, American biologist Stephen Kress started Project Puffin, bringing young puffins from Newfoundland to Eastern Egg Rock in Maine and using wooden decoys and mirrors to persuade returning birds the island was safe. It worked, and puffins now nest on several Maine islands again. The Atlantic puffin is Newfoundland and Labrador's provincial bird and a huge draw for tourism, from Witless Bay to Iceland's Westman Islands, where every summer local children rescue lost pufflings attracted to town lights.

north-american-beaver.anatomy: The beaver is North America's largest rodent. Its thick brown fur has two layers: long, coarse guard hairs and a dense, soft underfur that traps air and keeps the skin dry. Beavers comb oil from glands near their tail through their fur with a split claw on each hind foot. Their big, webbed hind feet push them through the water, while the small, nimble front paws carry sticks, mud and food. The famous tail is flat, scaly and wide; it works as a rudder, a prop to lean on while gnawing, a fat store for winter, and an alarm, slapped hard on the water to warn the family of danger. Beavers can close their lips behind their front teeth, so they can gnaw underwater without swallowing water, and valves close their ears and nostrils when they dive.
north-american-beaver.family: Beavers live in family groups, usually a breeding pair that stays together for many years, plus their young from this year and last year. Kits are born in late spring inside the lodge, typically two to four at a time. They have fur and open eyes at birth, and can swim within a day, though they cannot dive well at first because their fur is so buoyant. The whole family helps raise them: yearlings bring food and help repair the dam and lodge. Young beavers stay with their parents for about two years, learning to build, then leave to find their own territory, sometimes travelling many kilometres. Families mark their territory with mounds of mud scented with castoreum, a musky substance from glands near the tail, and keep strangers away.
north-american-beaver.people: The beaver shaped Canada's history. Beaver fur made a dense, waterproof felt prized for hats in Europe, and from the 1600s the fur trade drove exploration and settlement, founded companies like the Hudson's Bay Company, and changed the lives of many Indigenous peoples who trapped and traded furs. By the late 1800s beavers had been wiped out across much of the continent. Protection, reintroductions and the end of the fashion for beaver hats allowed them to return, and today there may be millions. Beavers can cause trouble, flooding roads and farmland, but many communities now use 'beaver deceivers', pipes that let water flow through a dam without the beavers noticing, so people and beavers can coexist. The beaver appears on the Canadian five-cent coin, and Parks Canada's logo features one.
